segments.text: We've had a lot of criticism in the community about the matrix and the process that's being used. We're trying to come up with the most objective process to evaluate applications. But we have another one before us for the first time. Nothing against the project, but I think we ought to continue item 8 and any other applications until October so we can apply the objective process. I think using the objective process will help us to get community buy-in on any kind of evaluation we do. In conversations with staff, there are a lot of questions. I sent out a memo last night with some of the questions that the problem with projects is being able to compare apples and apples. And there is a question about is it first in, first out, are we comparing over time? It is fair to everyone to take any new applications and put them in October so we're able to apply the new process.

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: Thank you very much. Board member Hurtak.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Thank you. The problem with that is that's not what we do in normal development. We aren't going to stop new projects in the rest of the city while we redo the land development code. But I don't think it's fair to the people who put in applications and followed the current rules to be punished to wait. I'm not comfortable with that.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson

I think the prudent thing to do, I get what you're saying. I agree with that, too. It's unfortunate. But I think where we are right now, it may be prudent to pause, get our heads about where the money is, what projects are in the pipeline, so we can make a really good decision further down the line.

Since Showmen's Rest listed the parcel of land within woodlawn cemetery in March of 2025, the potential buyer of the parcel of land had her camera disabled. Her security cameras were disabled. She received threatening letters in the mail, parked cars Across The Street from her home. Someone took it upon themselves to log on to a state website and filled out a historical cemetery form on a parcel of land zoned rs-50. John Perzia, president of Showmen's Rest, would have allowed a Gpr prior to what he calls public humiliation and three-ring circus, no pun intended. The one thing i've learned from saving cemeteries, it's always best to work together, not against one another. segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: Thank you, ma'am. We appreciate you. There being no further virtual public comment, we go to in person. When you come up, please state your name. My name is Mita Martinez. Everyone knows me as mimi. I live in ybor heights. I am a member of the East Tampa CAC Committee. I'm here today to support agenda item number 1 and number 8 because I do believe that it's going to benefit the community. In the community, there seems to be two schools of thoughts on these projects. One, there are people who believe that these projects will not benefit the community. And then the other big issue is money, and it's a concern for us and it's a concern for you. We are at a crossroads right now where for the first time the East Tampa CRA is getting a lot of developers who are interested in developing East Tampa. That is a good problem. But it's also opened up a can of worms as far as how do we diversify those funds so that every neighborhood in East Tampa feels like they are getting a little piece of that pie. Also, how do we know what is the best developer and what developer really has the community in mind. I do believe that there is an opportunity for us to have a more competitive special use grants application process to help us kind of navigate how we select who we're going to fund and how much we're going to fund. We have attracted developers to come to East Tampa, so I agree we should not slow that down and we need to strike while the iron is hot. But now we're at a crossroads. How do we evaluate who gets what. I don't subscribe to the thought where it is first come, first served. I don't. People are knocking at the door, and that is a good thing, but we also have to be very careful because you'll have bad characters who are knocking at that door, too. For me, when I see a developer who comes here and they lay out line by line how they are going to bring economic development into the community, how they are going to reduce slum and blight in an area that has been traditionally known for decades to be an area of drug dealing and prostitution, because the harsh reality, that is what the economic engine is on Nebraska Avenue. And that's hard to say, but it is. In the underworld, a lot of money is being made off of selling drugs and prostitution on Nebraska Avenue. Our barrier is we cannot tell private homeowners, hey, you can't sell drugs here, and we cannot go to the private business owners who own hotels, hey, you need to stop prostitution here. But we can bring in other types of development. That is our weapon to counter that, to bring in wholesome economic development that the people who live there will benefit from. So a lot of things for us to all think about. I appreciate what you do. I think we have some tough questions to ask, but I do think even as a CAC member, it could be very confusing for me as well as to who should I support and who I shouldn't. Thank you for your time.

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: Thank you, ma'am. We appreciate you. Next speaker, please. State your name. Bobby Creighton. Just wanted to briefly comment on the opening discussion you had this morning. Not only from the CRA but also from somebody taking that step and to venture into this territory. In terms of urban reworx project -- oh, running out of time. I'll stop there. Thank you.

segments.text: Thank you, Mr. Singer. Appreciate you, sir. Board member Maniscalco. What i'll do, guys, I think we do this under council, is five minutes for first round and then three minutes your second time speaking. Third time speaking, you get 10 seconds. Go ahead.

segments.text: My question will go to Mr. McCray. Mr. McCray, what is the ask here? What is the dollar amount?

segments.text: We had a long briefing yesterday, you and I. This could be one of several many projects. People are moving back to that community. Neighborhood Associations are strengthening each and every day. I heard about a Nebraska Avenue, like a business corridor that now exists. We've heard from residents. Ms. Martinez, Mr. Creighton was here. This is the beginning of a transformational positive, maybe a renaissance. We see what happened in Tampa Heights with armature works. And I think this is going to further expand it not just because of this project, but this is one of many that I hope come online. It needs it. We talk about affordable housing. Robin Lockett spoke. That's how I met her for the need of affordable housing. We've heard from a woman who is sitting in the back in the blue shirt, talking about the need for affordable housing. This isn't going to solve everything. This is a piece of the puzzle. I think 50 years, you put somebody in permanent housing, 50 years is a long time. I'm 41. That's me at 91, if I should live that long. Pastor Williams says 87 years old, we have to thank God for that. But this is something where people can have a place to live, sleep at night and not have to worry that they are going to be out on the street at a variety of different incomes. Yes, it's 20 units, but it's better than what was proposed before and we're touching more people and giving more opportunity. I want to support it, but I want to support it with the CAC said, $2 million and with the staff recommendation was. The 5 million, I get it. $5 million. But $2 million is what was recommended, it makes sense. That's where I want to be at. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: Thank you, board member Maniscalco. Now, in terms of folks to speak, I saw lights, first board member Miranda. I don't know which one of you all first. Go ahead, sir.

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: Times have changed. Things have changed. The problem is, you still have the same problem. Used to be three areas call Affordable Housing in Tampa when I was growing up in Tampa. Robles park, ponce de leon, and college hill. And they were always full. Always aligned to -- always a line to get in. I guess back when my parents applied, somehow they got in. They had to wait, but they got in. We had more kids to play with than ever before in every neighborhood. If you go back and do an interlocal study of those three, where are the residents, the child, the kids of the parents that went in there, you'll be amazed how many doctors and lawyers came out of there, how many professional people worked, how well they did in school, and i'm not talking about myself. So you can't say fund 20 years when you only have 8 years left. I'm not talking specific about this CRA. But you have to understand where we are at today. What happens if you do what they want to do to the next one that applies? Is it going to be 5 million or 10 million? I understand what's going on, but I want to make sure that the skin is played both ways from the CRA and from the developer. But how do those units come about, Robles park, college hill and ponce de leon? No CRAs then. Came from the Federal Government. That's how the Housing Authority came about. They are the ones that ran it. They had the offices, and they collected the rent. I don't know what the rent was, guarantee you, less than $40 a month. But things were different, but they are still the same. $40 a month then, now it's $400 a month now. Or more. So what i'm saying is, there's got to be a medium piece so that everybody can have an opportunity to live, no matter if it is 30, 40, 50, 60, 80, 100, because there's nothing affordable now. The reason I bought the house that I lived, horseback, 1968, that price of the house was 12,600. Three bedroom, one bath. The reason I bought that house because the payments would be $69 a month, include a second mortgage of $7 included in the $69. I didn't buy the one on Paris Street because it was $119. I remember the conversation with my wife. We could not afford 119. We could afford the 69. That's why I bought the house. Borrowed money from my uncle for the down payment. So what i'm saying, everybody has to have skin in the game. Family to help family. That's how I got my start. I'm saying that I'D like to continue this and make sure everybody has -- this administration, let me change railroad tracks for a minute. Has done more Affordable Housing than maybe the last two administrations put together. Not that they didn't want to do it. They had so many other priorities. Everything was shut down. No downtown. Ybor City was struggling, convention center was struggling. Everybody was struggling. So they didn't have the capital to do it. The one I feel most for, Mayor Iorio. Took office with nothing to do, no money to spend and did a marvelous job of running the city. Yes, lay off 750 some employees of the City Of Tampa. But she had the courage to do that to bring it back. If she hadn't done that, we would still be in the hole. We have to be careful how we do it. Not against the project, but the $5 million scares the hell out of me because it will be something greater after this.

segments.text: That is higher than normal, correct. That is higher than normal. segments.text: I might cut you off sometimes and I apologize in advance. They are putting me to a timer. I want to move and ask additional questions. segments.text: Good afternoon, board members. As you can see here, the 30% allocation for 2026 goes as follows: for central park, we have $604,000. For channel CRA roughly around 4 million. segments.text: Any questions from board members? Board member Clendenin.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: I don't support making it a requirement allocation. I don't support the 30% requirement. I think this should be a budgetary item and flexible with the actual needs and the fiscal responsibility of budgeting. While I do support allocating 46% in the budget, I don't think it necessarily needs to be a requirement. Each board member needs to make that determination based on how the budgets are presented. It's interesting because the Tampa Heights example is a classic example why an arbitrary number like 30% just doesn't work. We put a requirement on a CRA that is fiscally impossible for them to meet. Again, I get that my good friend Mr. Dingfelder and a couple other councilpersons thought this was a good idea at the time, as it matured and moved on, we probably should revisit this at some point. Two great examples. Want to put more money in East Tampa. Tampa Heights doesn't work, and we're kind of boxing in money that could be higher and better use and others that maybe we could, again, swap out for general fund money and move some money back into these areas where we can afford it, West Tampa, East Tampa, can afford to build much more for much less. segments.text: My next motion, something i've been toying around with, I wanted to, frankly, wait until after session to propose this.
